291.quote_or_event: “Do not utter even a single harsh word; your True Lord and Master abides in all.”
291.explanation: In his saloks Sheikh Farid tells the seeker never to wound anyone with speech, because God dwells in every heart.
291.tie_back: The Kural defines truthful speech as speech that harms no one in any way. Farid grounds the same ideal of harmless speech in God's presence in all beings.
291.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Salok Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
291._accuracy_note: A strong fit on speech that harms no one. Farid speaks of harshness, not of truthfulness as such, and he is a Bhagat whose verses are in the Granth, not a Guru.

292.quote_or_event: “Kabeer, where there is spiritual wisdom, there is righteousness and Dharma. Where there is falsehood, there is sin.”
292.explanation: In his saloks Bhagat Kabir sets falsehood plainly on the side of sin. Gurbani as a whole treats kooR (falsehood) as the wall between the soul and God.
292.tie_back: The Kural allows that a falsehood can stand in the place of truth if it produces faultless good. Gurbani offers no such exception, which makes this verse a point of contrast rather than agreement.
292.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1372, Salok Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
292._accuracy_note: A candid contrast, not a parallel: I found no SGGS passage that permits a beneficial falsehood, and this verse places falsehood squarely with sin.

293.quote_or_event: “Speaking lies, one eats poison; the self-willed manmukh departs, crying out in pain.”
293.explanation: In a salok of the Vaar in Raag Raamkalee, Guru Amar Das says that the liar feeds himself poison. The self-willed person (manmukh) who lives by falsehood leaves the world in anguish.
293.tie_back: The Kural warns that a lie told against what one's own heart knows will burn that heart. Guru Amar Das likewise makes the lie a poison taken by the liar himself.
293.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 948, Raag Raamkalee (Ramkali ki Vaar, salok), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
293._accuracy_note: A strong fit on the lie harming the liar from within. Gurbani does not specify a lie told against one's own knowledge, and its image is poison rather than burning.

294.quote_or_event: “One knows the Truth only when the Truth is in his heart.”
294.explanation: In a salok of Asa di Vaar, Guru Nanak says truth is real only when it lives in the heart, not merely on the tongue.
294.tie_back: The Kural promises that one who is free of falsehood even in the heart will live in the hearts of all people. Guru Nanak shares the first half: truth must first dwell in one's own heart.
294.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 468, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
294._accuracy_note: Next-best: the verse matches the Kural's demand for truth in the heart but not its promise of being cherished by everyone.

295.quote_or_event: “Pilgrimages, austere discipline, compassion and charity - these, by themselves, bring only an iota of merit.”
295.explanation: In Japji Guru Nanak says that the recognised religious works, including austerity and charity, earn only a sesame-seed's worth of honour. What counts is hearing, believing and loving the Name within.
295.tie_back: The Kural ranks truthful speech that agrees with the heart above those who practise both austerity and charity. Japji likewise puts austerity and charity below the inner relation with the True One.
295.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 4, Japji Sahib, Pauri 21, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
295._accuracy_note: A strong structural match: both rank austerity and charity below something inward. Japji's higher good is love of the Name, of which truthfulness is part but not the whole.

296.quote_or_event: “Truth is the medicine for all; it removes and washes away our sins.”
296.explanation: In the same salok of Asa di Vaar on what true living means, Guru Nanak calls Truth a cure for every ill, cleansing the person of wrongdoing.
296.tie_back: The Kural says truthfulness brings every other virtue with it, without strain. Guru Nanak makes truth the single remedy that heals everything else.
296.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 468, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
296._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit on truth as the one source of all goodness. The Kural's theme of fame is absent, and Gurbani's sach also means the True Lord, not only truthful conduct.

297.quote_or_event: “So how can you become truthful? And how can the veil of illusion be torn away? O Nanak, it is written that you shall obey the Hukam of His Command, and walk in the Way of His Will.”
297.explanation: Japji's first pauri rejects ritual bathing, silence, fasting and cleverness as paths to becoming truthful (sachiaara). It names one way only: living in the divine order.
297.tie_back: The Kural says that if one practises truthfulness unfailingly, it is well even without other virtuous deeds. Japji likewise treats becoming truthful as the one thing needed and finds the many other practices unnecessary.
297.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Japji Sahib, Pauri 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
297._accuracy_note: Next-best: both make truthfulness the single sufficient aim. Japji reaches it through obedience to Hukam rather than unfailing truthful speech, and it dismisses ritual rather than virtuous deeds.

298.quote_or_event: “One knows the Truth only when the Truth is in his heart. The filth of falsehood departs, and the body is washed clean.”
298.explanation: In Asa di Vaar Guru Nanak describes true cleansing as truth entering the heart and washing out the filth of falsehood. Elsewhere Gurbani repeatedly rejects ritual bathing as a means of purity.
298.tie_back: The Kural says water purifies outwardly but truthfulness shows inner purity. Guru Nanak makes the same contrast: falsehood is the real dirt, and truth is what washes it away.
298.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 468, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
298._accuracy_note: A near one-to-one match on truth as the cleanser of inner impurity. Gurbani's sach includes the True Lord dwelling within, a theistic sense the Kural does not state.

299.quote_or_event: “If a hundred moons were to rise, and a thousand suns appeared, even with such light, there would still be pitch darkness without the Guru.”
299.explanation: In a salok in Asa di Vaar, Guru Angad says that no amount of outward light can lift inner darkness. Only the Guru's light can do that.
299.tie_back: The Kural says not every lamp is a true lamp, and for the wise only the lamp of truthfulness is real. Guru Angad likewise sets countless outer lights against the one inner light that truly dispels darkness.
299.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 463, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
299._accuracy_note: A strong structural match: many outer lights against one true inner light. In Gurbani the true light is the Guru, whose word is truth, not truthfulness itself.

300.quote_or_event: “Truth is higher than everything; but higher still is truthful living.”
300.explanation: In a hymn in Siree Raag, Guru Nanak gives his verdict that Truth surpasses all else and that living truthfully (sach aachaar) ranks higher still. This is one of the best-known lines in Sikh ethics.
300.tie_back: The Kural closes with Valluvar's own verdict that among all things found to be real, nothing is better than truthfulness. Guru Nanak gives the same judgement: nothing ranks above truth lived out.
300.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 62, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
300._accuracy_note: A near one-to-one match: both are first-person verdicts placing truth above everything. Guru Nanak adds a distinction between truth and truthful conduct that the Kural does not draw.
